summary: Some JOSE and COSE algorithm identifiers leave details, such as the curve or hash, to be inferred from other information. This specification defines fully-specified identifiers that state every choice. It updates RFC 7518, RFC 8037 and RFC 9053, which define earlier algorithm identifiers.

plainLanguage.summary: When two programs agree on a cryptographic algorithm by name, the name has to say everything they need to know. Some names did not. This document registers new names that leave nothing out, and marks the old ones as not to be used.

subtitle: Algorithm names for JOSE and COSE that state every choice, so negotiation by name alone actually works.

tldr.problem: Many protocols negotiate cryptography using only algorithm identifiers, but polymorphic identifiers such as EdDSA or COSE ES256 do not say which curve is used, so negotiation can fail.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9864 registers fully-specified identifiers such as Ed25519, Ed448 and ESP256 for JOSE and COSE, deprecates the polymorphic ones they replace, and tells registry experts to accept only fully-specified identifiers in future.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now use fully-specified identifiers for ECDSA and EdDSA signatures; RSA, ECDH and HSS-LMS identifiers were left alone for now.

today: RFC 9864 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025. It updates RFC 7518, RFC 8037 and RFC 9053, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Fully Specified and Polymorphic
sections.content:
The IANA algorithm registries for JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) contain two kinds of algorithm identifier.

A fully specified identifier fully determines the cryptographic operations to be performed, including any curve, key derivation function and hash function. Examples are RS256 and ES256K in both JOSE and COSE, and ES256 in JOSE. A polymorphic identifier requires information beyond the identifier to determine the operations, and that extra information could include the actual key value and the curve it uses. Examples are the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm EdDSA in both JOSE and COSE, and ES256 in COSE.

This matters because many protocols negotiate supported operations using only algorithm identifiers. OAuth Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414) uses negotiation parameters like token_endpoint_auth_signing_alg_values_supported, OpenID Connect Discovery negotiates using alg and enc values, and W3C Web Authentication and the FIDO Client to Authenticator Protocol negotiate using COSE alg numbers. None of this works for polymorphic algorithms: with EdDSA it is not known which of the curves Ed25519 and Ed448 are supported, and that causes real problems in practice.

WebAuthn contains a de facto workaround, redefining the COSE EdDSA algorithm identifier so that it means Ed25519 only. That makes algorithm negotiation succeed, but it also effectively eliminates the possibility of using Ed448. Other similar workarounds are used in practice.

Using fully specified algorithms is sometimes referred to as the 'cipher suite' approach, and using polymorphic algorithms as the 'a la carte' approach. This specification creates fully specified algorithm identifiers for the registered polymorphic JOSE and COSE algorithms and their parameters, enabling applications to use only fully specified identifiers, and it deprecates the practice of registering polymorphic algorithm identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: Some algorithm names say everything needed to run them, and others leave a choice for the user to make. When two programs pick a name from a list, a name with a hidden choice in it can make them disagree without either being wrong.

sections.title: New Signature Identifiers
sections.content:
The COSE algorithm registrations for ECDSA are polymorphic, because they do not specify the curve used: ES256 is defined as 'ECDSA w/ SHA-256'. The corresponding JOSE registrations in RFC 7518 are already fully specified.

This document defines seven fully specified COSE ECDSA algorithms. ESP256, with value -9, uses the P-256 curve and SHA-256; ESP384, with value -51, uses the P-384 curve and SHA-384; ESP512, with value -52, uses the P-521 curve and SHA-512. The three P-curve algorithms are marked Recommended. Four more use the Brainpool curves and are not marked Recommended: ESB256 with value -265 uses BrainpoolP256r1 and SHA-256, ESB320 with value -266 uses BrainpoolP320r1 and SHA-384, ESB384 with value -267 uses BrainpoolP384r1 and SHA-384, and ESB512 with value -268 uses BrainpoolP512r1 and SHA-512.

For EdDSA, RFC 8037 registers a polymorphic JOSE identifier and RFC 9053 a polymorphic COSE one. This document adds Ed25519, with COSE value -19, defined by the Ed25519 parameter set in Section 5.1 of RFC 8032, and Ed448, with COSE value -53, defined by the Ed448 parameter set in Section 5.2 of the same document. Both are Optional for JOSE and Recommended for COSE.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one name that could mean several things, each combination of curve and hash now gets its own name and its own number, so two programs cannot pick different meanings from the same name.

sections.title: Fully Specified Encryption
sections.content:
Using fully specified encryption algorithms enables the sender and the receiver to agree on all mandatory security parameters. They also enable protocols to specify an allow list of algorithm combinations that contains no polymorphic combination, which prevents problems such as cross-curve key establishment, cross-protocol symmetric encryption, or a mismatch between the key derivation function size and the symmetric key.

Both JOSE and COSE have operations that take several algorithms as parameters. An encrypted object in JOSE uses two identifiers: the first in the alg header parameter, which says how to determine the content encryption key, and the second in the enc header parameter, which says the content encryption algorithm. Encrypted COSE objects use several algorithms for the same purposes.

To perform fully specified encryption in JOSE, the alg value MUST specify all parameters for key establishment or derive some of them from the accompanying enc value, and the enc value MUST specify all parameters for symmetric encryption. Encryption using an alg value of A128KW and an enc value of A128GCM is fully specified. In JOSE there is the option to derive some cryptographic parameters used in the alg computation from the accompanying enc value; for example the keydatalen parameter for ECDH-ES is determined from the enc value. For the purposes of an alg value being fully specified, deriving parameters from enc does not make the algorithm polymorphic, because the computation is still fully determined by the algorithm identifiers used. That option is not present in COSE, where the outer alg value MUST specify all parameters for key establishment and the inner alg value MUST specify all parameters for symmetric encryption. When using COSE_Encrypt, the outer alg is in the headers of the COSE_Encrypt object and the inner alg is in the headers of the COSE_recipient object.

Most registered encryption algorithms are already fully specified. All the symmetric encryption algorithms registered by RFC 7518 and RFC 9053 are, as are all the registered key wrapping algorithms and the algorithms performing key wrapping using AES GCM. The JOSE dir and COSE direct algorithms are fully specified, as are the COSE direct+HKDF algorithms and the JOSE algorithms performing key encryption with PBES2. The Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key establishment algorithms in both JOSE and COSE are polymorphic, because they do not specify the elliptic curve to be used for the key, whether the ephemeral key of the Ephemeral-Static algorithms or the static key of the Static-Static algorithms registered by COSE.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypting something takes two choices: how the key travels and how the content is locked. Both choices have to be spelled out, and a protocol can then refuse combinations it does not trust.

sections.title: Registrations and Review Rules
sections.content:
IANA registered Ed25519 and Ed448 in the JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms registry, with the alg usage location, an implementation requirement of Optional, and this document as an additional reference for the registry. It marked the polymorphic JOSE EdDSA registration as Deprecated.

In the COSE Algorithms registry, IANA registered the seven ECDSA names and Ed25519 and Ed448, with a capability of kty, and marked the polymorphic COSE registrations ES256 with value -7, ES384 with value -35, ES512 with value -36 and EdDSA with value -8 as Deprecated.

The review instructions for the designated experts of both registries gain an additional criterion: only fully specified algorithm identifiers may be registered, and polymorphic algorithm identifiers must not be registered.

Section 4.4 defines two terms that JOSE and COSE had used without defining. Deprecated means there is a preferred mechanism to achieve similar functionality, that this replacement SHOULD be used in new deployments in preference to the deprecated identifier, unless documented operational or regulatory requirements prevent migration. Prohibited means the identifier and the functionality it references MUST NOT be used, and identifiers may be designated as prohibited because of security flaws. The set of values for the COSE Recommended column is now Yes, No, Filter Only, Prohibited and Deprecated. The definitions were chosen because they are consistent with all existing registrations in both registries, and the only net change is to enable a clear distinction between Deprecated and Prohibited in future COSE registrations.
sections.plainLanguage: The official lists get new entries, the old vague ones are marked 'please do not use for new things', and from now on only precise names may be added.

sections.title: Keys and Algorithms Left Alone
sections.content:
The key representations for the new fully specified algorithms are the same as those for the polymorphic algorithms they replace, other than the alg value if one is included. A key used with Ed25519 is represented as in RFC 8037, except that the alg value would be Ed25519 rather than EdDSA.

Some existing polymorphic algorithms are not updated. There are different points of view on whether RS256, RS384 and RS512 should be considered fully specified, because they can operate on keys of different sizes, for instance both 2048- and 4096-bit keys, and the same is true of the PS* algorithms. This document neither describes nor requests registration of any fully specified RSA algorithms, although some implementations, such as FIPS-compliant hardware security modules, limit RSA key parameters to specific values, and a future specification could always register RSA identifiers that are specific to particular key characteristics.

The ECDH algorithms are not updated either. The registered JOSE and COSE ECDH algorithms are polymorphic because they do not specify the curve to be used for the ephemeral key. Fully specified versions would specify all the choices needed, including the key derivation function and the curve, so an algorithm performing ECDH-ES using the Concat KDF and the P-256 curve could be defined and registered, but this specification does not do so and other specifications could.

The HSS-LMS algorithm registered by COSE is polymorphic because the identifier does not specify the hash function to be used. Like ECDH, this specification does not register replacement algorithms, but future specifications could do so.
sections.plainLanguage: Some names were left as they were for now. The authors say a later document can fix them if people need it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for ECDSA in RFC 7518, for EdDSA in RFC 8037, and for ECDSA and EdDSA in RFC 9053 apply, as do the security considerations for preventing cross-protocol attacks described in RFC 9459.

An attack signature is a unique pattern or characteristic used to identify malicious activity, enabling systems to detect and respond to known threats. The digital signature and key establishment algorithms used by software can contribute to an attack signature. By varying the identifier used for an algorithm, some software systems may attempt to evade rule-based detection and classification, so those systems may need new rules for fully specified algorithms. Writing rules for polymorphic algorithms is harder, because each variant must be accounted for: ES384 in COSE might be used with three different keys, each with a different curve.

A cryptographic key MUST be used with only a single algorithm unless the use of the same key with different algorithms is proven secure. It is therefore RECOMMENDED that the algorithm parameter of JSON Web Keys and COSE Keys be present, unless there is some other mechanism that ensures the key is used as intended.

In COSE, cross-protocol attacks can be prevented in two ways: by allowing only authenticated content encryption algorithms, or by binding the potentially unauthenticated content encryption algorithm to the key protection algorithm, so that different content encryption algorithms result in different content encryption keys. Which choice to use in which circumstances is beyond the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Use each key for one job only, and say which job, so nobody can trick it into doing another.
